newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New-look Asian fuel oil futures win trade blessing.
newsitem.headline: New-look Asian fuel oil futures win trade blessing.

text.p: A new-look fuel oil futures contract for the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) received a warm -- if not emphatic -- blessing from oil traders on Tuesday.
"I will be dissappointed if after the change, the contract is not up and running," one trader said.
SIMEX said on Tuesday it planned to list a revised fuel oil contract on April 22. It said the changes have the endorsement of the trading community.
"After meeting with SIMEX over a six-month period, hashing out revisions for the contract, I certainly will trade on it and hope for the best," said a Japanese trader based in Singapore.
Most traders said the fuel oil market would benefit from a futures market, which would act as a price benchmark outside of the industry price assessment publications used heavily used at the moment.
An alternative would provide greater price transparency and accuracy for the market, they said.
But while major oil companies have pledged support for the revised futures contract, independent oil traders were more cautious.
"We will see how it goes before putting our money in it," one independent trader said.

A fuel oil contract has been listed on SIMEX since 1989 but has effectively been untraded since 1995 when traders said the specifications of the contract fell out of line with the underlying physical market.
The revisions are aimed at pumping life into the dormant market.
Asia has a long line of failed futures contracts in the energy sector. A gas oil futures market, a contract on benchmark Dubai crude oil have died through lack of trade support.

SIMEX currently lists a Brent crude futures contract, which can be traded in Singapore or on London's International Petroleum Exchange. But the lack of traded volume in Singapore has led to worries that the contract will not survive.
The latest attempt to keep the fuel oil contract alive includes a number of changes to specifications, aimed at bringing the contract into line with physical fuel oil that is traded in Singapore.
"SIMEX hopes that traders would use the revised contract as a hedging tool, an additional option to hedge their risks over the existing over-the-counter trades," a western trader said.
SIMEX officials have been meeting officials of major oil companies, traders and bunker players since June to revive the flagging fuel oil contract, which was first listed in 1989.

On its debut, SIMEX fuel oil contract trades a daily average volume of nearly 5,000 lots. But the volume dwindled to a mere 162 lots per day in 1995. Since August 1995, it has been virtually in limbo.
The SIMEX fuel oil contract allows traders to hedge financial exposure on positions they have in the physical market and also allows them to receive physical cargoes of fuel oil.

Traders said the illiquidity of the existing fuel oil contract was due to fuel oil specifications that were not in line with underlying cash market, trade manipulation and the preference for the unregulated over the counter trades (OTC).
